children: Talk to Chuck? Investors may want to chat with "Charley" instead. That is the name of Charles Schwab's new artificial intelligence chatbot for customers that the company plans to begin rolling out next month. It's the latest move by a brokerage firm to offer customers AI-powered tools and assistants.

Schwab says Charley can help customers find information, get answers to their questions, and complete certain tasks such as updating watchlists, enrolling eligible securities in dividend reinvestment, and adding beneficiaries. Currently, it won't execute trades on demand. The company says the client remains in control of the agent, which also requires confirmation before it takes actions. Customers can converse with Charley through voice or text, the company says.
The agent is powered by large language models, which Schwab declined to name. Schwab employees participated in a pilot to test and refine the AI assistant, the company says.

Schwab also has plans to provide AI capabilities to registered investment advisors, who rely on Schwab to provide them with a trading platform and safeguard client assets on their behalf. Schwab is the nation's largest custodian for RIAs. In September, Schwab said it was partnering with Anthropic to connect Claude for Financial Advisors, a suite of AI-powered tools, to its data, including balances, positions, and transactions.

Other financial services companies have been launching AI assistants of their own. For example, SoFi Technologies' personal finance assistant, SoFi Coach, launched in June. The company says SoFi Coach can provide customers with guidance and assistance with tasks such as budgeting and managing debt.

Charley comes as investors fret repeatedly over whether AI is a boon or a threat to brokerage firms. In late September, brokerage stocks took a licking when Meta's new personal AI assistant, Muse, revived concerns it would enable  cash-sorting. That is a process by which customers move cash from brokerage sweep accounts that pay little in interest to customers (but which are profitable for brokerage firms) to higher yielding options elsewhere. On Tuesday Sept. 22, shares of Schwab and LPL Financial dropped 6% and 7.4%, respectively.

Schwab's stock was down 0.6% on Wednesday afternoon, sliding alongside shares of other financial services companies. The Vanguard Financials ETF, which tracks a broad basket of financial stocks, was down 0.79% and the benchmark S&P 500 was up 0.4%.
